topic: Transfer of command and initial response

notes.front: What is Transfer of command, in one sentence?
notes.back: The process of moving responsibility for incident command from one Incident Commander to another.
notes.explanation: Incident command is built so command can change hands with minimal disruption to the ongoing response.
notes.example: Like a relay runner handing off the baton without the race stopping.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual, Lesson 7, Visual 2, SM-217

notes.front: Which reason for transferring command involves a jurisdiction or agency being legally required to take over?
notes.explanation: Transfer of command can happen for several distinct reasons, not only when an incident grows in complexity.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual, Lesson 7, Visual 3, SM-218

notes.front: Which reason for transferring command involves changing command purely for effectiveness or efficiency?
notes.explanation: Transfer of command can happen for several distinct reasons, not only when an incident grows in complexity.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual, Lesson 7, Visual 3, SM-218

notes.front: Which reason for transferring command involves the incident's complexity changing?

notes.front: Which reason for transferring command involves the current IC's personal emergency?
notes.explanation: Transfer of command can happen for several distinct reasons, not only when an incident grows in complexity.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual, Lesson 7, Visual 3, SM-218

notes.front: Which reason for transferring command involves the Agency Administrator or Jurisdictional Executive directing the change?

notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual, Lesson 7, Visual 3, SM-218

notes.front: If a more qualified person arrives on scene, must command automatically transfer to them?
notes.back: No: they may assume command per agency guidelines, maintain command and monitor, or request a more qualified Incident Commander.
notes.explanation: The arrival of a more qualified person is a choice point, not an automatic trigger for transfer.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual, Lesson 7, Visual 5, SM-220

notes.front: Whenever possible, how should transfer of command take place?
notes.back: Face-to-face, with a complete briefing, and with the effective time and date communicated to all personnel.
notes.explanation: A face-to-face briefing captures information a written note alone would miss, reducing disruption to the response.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual, Lesson 7, Visual 6, SM-221

notes.front: Which transfer-of-command briefing element covers the current situation status?
notes.explanation: A transfer of command briefing should always take place and cover every one of these elements.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual, Lesson 7, Visual 8, SM-223

notes.front: What can the initial Incident Commander use to document actions and situational information for a transfer of command?
notes.explanation: For more complex transfers, every aspect of the incident must be documented, not only what fits on Form 201.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual, Lesson 7, Visual 9, SM-226

notes.front: What must the first person on scene explicitly do about command?
notes.back: Explicitly establish incident or Unified Command, and clearly state and record when command is transferred.
notes.explanation: Command does not start automatically; someone must actively declare and record it, from the very first arrival.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual, Lesson 8, Visual 8, SM-239

notes.front: As an incident grows more complex, what can happen to the initial Incident Commander?
notes.back: They may continue as a member of a Unified Command, or more senior personnel may be appointed to command.
notes.explanation: Growth in complexity does not always remove the original Incident Commander; it can simply widen command to include others.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual, Lesson 8, Visual 36, SM-271

notes.front: A tired Incident Commander formally hands responsibility to a fresh Incident Commander for the next shift. What process is this?
notes.explanation: Any time responsibility for incident command moves from one Incident Commander to another, it is a transfer of command.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual, Lesson 7, Visual 2, SM-217

notes.front: A hurricane response is now expected to run for three more weeks, and the current Incident Commander needs a break. What reason for transferring command applies?
notes.back: The need to relieve personnel on incidents of extended duration.
notes.explanation: Extended incidents are physically and mentally demanding, so planned relief is one of the recognised reasons to transfer command.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual, Lesson 7, Visual 3, SM-218

notes.front: A senior, highly qualified chief arrives at a small, well-managed incident already led by a junior officer. What should happen to command?
notes.back: No automatic transfer: the chief may assume command under agency guidelines, leave command as is and monitor, or request a more qualified IC.
notes.choices:
A) Command automatically transfers to the senior chief
B) The senior chief has three options and must choose one
C) Command stays exactly as it is and nothing changes
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: the arrival of a more qualified person never transfers command automatically. C is wrong: the senior chief must still actively decide to assume, monitor, or request, even if the choice is to keep monitoring.
notes.explanation: Seniority alone is not a rule for transfer: agency guidelines, not rank, decide what happens next.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual, Lesson 7, Visual 5, SM-220

notes.front: Two supervisors swap by radio only, with no shared briefing and no announced effective time. What part of the transfer of command procedure did they skip?
notes.back: A face-to-face briefing, and communicating the effective time and date to all personnel.
notes.explanation: Skipping the briefing and the announced effective time raises the risk that other responders act on outdated information.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual, Lesson 7, Visual 6, SM-221

notes.front: An incoming Incident Commander is told the current objectives but nothing about resources already ordered or en route. What briefing element was missed?
notes.explanation: Missing this element risks the incoming Commander not knowing what is already on its way, and possibly duplicating orders.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual, Lesson 7, Visual 8, SM-223

notes.front: A first-arriving officer wants a standard form to record initial actions and situational information before handing off command. What should they use?
notes.explanation: It is the standard tool for capturing that early information so it survives the transfer to the next Incident Commander.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual, Lesson 7, Visual 9, SM-226

notes.front: A firefighter arrives first at a multi-vehicle crash but never states aloud that she is taking command. What NIMS Management Characteristic has she failed to apply?
notes.back: Establishment and Transfer of Command: command must be explicitly established, not assumed silently.
notes.explanation: Silent, unstated command creates confusion about who is actually in charge and accountable.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual, Lesson 8, Visual 8, SM-239
